"Leech" has three distinct meanings as a noun: an animal, a type of person, and a sailing term.

A leech is a type of worm, but not the kind you find in garden soil. It is a parasitic worm — meaning it survives by living on or in another creature (called a "host") and feeding off it, while giving nothing back and often causing harm.

Most leeches live in freshwater environments — ponds, rivers, lakes, swamps, and marshes. A smaller number live in damp soil or in the ocean.

What does a leech look like?

A leech has a soft, slightly flat, stretchy body. It is divided into segments (ring-like sections), which you can sometimes see along its body. Most leeches are dark-colored — black, dark brown, or olive green. Their size varies widely: some are just a few millimeters long, while others can grow to 20 centimeters or more. A leech has two suckers — one at each end of its body. The rear sucker is mainly used for gripping surfaces. The front sucker is where its mouth is, and it's the one used for feeding.

How does a leech feed?

This is the most important thing to understand about a leech. Most leech species feed on blood. Here's how the process works:

First, the leech crawls onto the skin of a host — which can be a human, a frog, a fish, a deer, a bird, or many other animals. It uses its front sucker to press firmly against the skin. It then bites through the skin, but this bite is usually completely painless. You often don't even feel it. This is because the leech releases a numbing substance when it bites, which prevents you from feeling any discomfort.

Once it has broken through the skin, it begins to suck blood. It also releases a special chemical called hirudin into your bloodstream. Hirudin is an anticoagulant — a substance that stops blood from clotting (thickening and sealing up). Normally, when you get a cut, your blood quickly clots to stop the bleeding. The leech's hirudin blocks this, so your blood keeps flowing freely while the leech feeds. This is very clever from the leech's point of view — it ensures an uninterrupted meal.

The leech stays attached and feeds slowly and steadily for anywhere from 20 minutes to well over an hour. During this time, it can consume several times its own body weight in blood — it stretches and expands enormously as it fills up. Once it is full, it simply lets go and falls off. After a large meal like this, a leech can go weeks or even months without needing to eat again.

One important side effect: because of the hirudin left in your skin, the bite wound keeps bleeding for a while after the leech has gone — sometimes for several hours. It is not dangerous, but it can be alarming if you don't know why it's happening.

Are all leeches blood-suckers?

Not all of them. Some leeches are predators rather than parasites — they hunt and swallow small invertebrates (like worms, insect larvae, and snails) whole. However, the blood-sucking behavior is what defines the word "leech" in common understanding, and it is what gives rise to all the word's other meanings.

For centuries — right up into the 1800s — doctors believed that many diseases were caused by having too much blood in the body, or blood that had gone "bad." Their main treatment was to remove blood from the patient's body. This practice was called bloodletting.

Leeches were one of the primary tools used for this. A doctor would place several leeches directly on a patient's skin — on the forehead, the neck, the chest, the back, wherever seemed appropriate — and let them feed. The goal was to drain what was believed to be harmful or excess blood. Leeches were applied to treat fevers, headaches, skin conditions, mental illness, infections, and nearly every other ailment you can think of.

This practice was so deeply connected to medicine that the word "leech" was itself an old word for doctor or healer during medieval times.

We now understand that bloodletting was almost always useless and frequently made patients weaker and sicker, not better. It was based on a completely wrong theory of how the human body works. Many patients died or suffered needlessly as a result.

Here is one of the more surprising facts about this word: leeches are still used in medicine today, but for reasons that are genuinely sound and scientifically validated.

After certain surgeries — particularly surgeries where a body part has been reattached (such as a severed finger or ear being sewn back on) or where skin has been reconstructed or grafted — a serious problem can arise. Blood can pool and clot in the reattached tissue. When this happens, fresh, oxygenated blood cannot get through, and the tissue begins to die. This is a major surgical complication.

Leeches solve this problem in two ways at once. First, they physically drain the pooled, stagnant blood. Second, the hirudin they release keeps blood flowing properly and prevents further clotting in the area. This gives the body time to grow new blood vessels and restore normal circulation.

The specific species used for this is called the medicinal leech (Hirudo medicinalis). This use is fully approved and recognized in mainstream modern medicine. In fact, medicinal leeches are classified as a medical device by regulatory authorities. They are bred in sterile conditions specifically for surgical use. It sounds strange, but they genuinely help save tissue and, in some cases, entire limbs.

When you call a person a leech, you are using the word as a strong criticism or insult. The meaning maps directly onto the animal: just as the worm latches onto a host and drains its blood while giving nothing back, a person who is a "leech" takes from others constantly without giving anything in return.

A leech, in this sense, is someone who:

  • Borrows money repeatedly but never repays it.
  • Lives off someone else's income, home, or resources without contributing.
  • Always asks for favors but is never available when you need help.
  • drains your time, energy, or generosity while benefiting themselves.
  • Takes credit for other people's work.

The core idea is one-sided taking. The leech benefits; the person being leeched off loses something. There is no balance, no reciprocity, no fairness.

Some examples of how it is used in a sentence:

  • "He stayed on her couch for six months and never paid a cent — a total leech."
  • "Once you become successful, leeches will start coming out of the woodwork."
  • "I had to cut him off; he was a leech on my time and money."

You can also use it as a verb — "to leech off someone" — meaning to behave in this way toward them. But as a noun, "a leech" refers to the person themselves.

This meaning is quite specialized and used mainly in the world of sailing and boat-building. In sailing, the leech is the back (trailing) edge of a sail — the edge that faces away from the mast and away from the direction the wind is coming from.

To picture this: think of a triangular sail on a modern sailboat. It has three edges. The luff is the front edge — the one attached to the mast or a wire. The foot is the bottom edge. And the leech is the remaining edge — the back, or trailing, edge that faces the stern (back) of the boat.

On older rectangular (square) sails, the term applies to both of the vertical side edges, so such a sail has two leeches, one on each side.

Sailors, boat designers, and sail-makers use this term routinely when talking about the shape, tension, and trimming of sails. Getting the leech of a sail to curve or lie in a particular way has a real effect on how efficiently the sail catches and channels the wind. A sail with a leech that flaps or twists incorrectly can noticeably reduce a boat's speed and control.

The single most powerful idea connecting all of these meanings is one-way taking with nothing given back. The animal does it biologically. The historical doctor used the animal to do it medically (if misguidedly). The modern surgeon uses the animal to do it beneficially. The person does it socially. Even the sailing term — the leech of a sail — is the edge that "trails," that follows, that takes from the wind's force.

When you hear or read the word "leech," context will almost always make it immediately clear which meaning is intended. In everyday conversation, it will nearly always be either the animal (especially in nature, biology, or outdoor contexts) or the figurative person (in social contexts). The medical and nautical meanings appear in their specific professional domains.
